samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A multi-year project to restore the natural flow of Cripple Creek near Fairbanks, Alaska, culminated in success, nearly 90 years after its channel was diverted in 1935 for hydraulic mining operations. [2, 3, 4] The restoration, a partnership led by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and the Interior Alaska Land Trust, aimed to improve rearing habitat for juvenile Chinook salmon and other native fish, which was poor in the artificial, channelized drain. [2, 4] The comprehensive effort, which began in 2017, involved replacing and retrofitting multiple road culverts to allow for fish passage and ultimately redirecting water back into the historic channel. [3, 4] Key partners included the Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities, the University of Alaska-Fairbanks, local students, and community landowners. [4, 6] After a setback in 2020 when an initial diversion structure washed out, a successful implementation in the late summer and autumn of 2022 allowed clean water to flow through the creek's original channel for the first time in over 80 years. [4, 6, 7] By the spring of 2023, the historic channel was fully reconnected to the Chena River, marking a significant milestone in restoring the area's aquatic habitat. [6] <2> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) released the final report for the 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation on October 12, 2023. [1, 2] The survey, conducted in partnership with the Association of Fish & Wildlife Agencies and NORC at the University of Chicago, revealed that 148.3 million U.S. residents aged 16 and older participated in wildlife-watching activities. [4, 8] Additionally, 39.9 million people engaged in fishing and 14.4 million in hunting. [2, 4, 8] These recreational activities contributed significantly to the U.S. economy, with participants spending an estimated $394 to $395 billion on equipment, travel, licenses, and fees. [1, 2, 3, 7] The 2022 survey, which has been conducted approximately every five years since 1955, was redesigned to reduce respondent burden and increase accuracy, including a new web-based response option. [1, 5, 7] Consequently, its results are not directly comparable to previous surveys. [1] <3> On October 10, 2023, the Department of the Interior announced the establishment of two new national wildlife refuges, the 569th and 570th units in the National Wildlife Refuge System. [3, 6, 11] The new refuges are the Wyoming Toad Conservation Area in Wyoming and the Paint Rock River National Wildlife Refuge in Tennessee. [3, 6] The creation of these refuges aims to conserve crucial habitats, protect threatened and endangered species, and increase public access to outdoor recreational activities like hunting, fishing, and hiking. [3, 7, 12] The Wyoming Toad Conservation Area, encompassing 1,078 acres, is particularly vital for the Wyoming toad, one of North America's most endangered amphibians. [7, 15] The 87-acre Paint Rock River National Wildlife Refuge in Tennessee will protect a watershed that is home to 100 species of fish and 50 types of freshwater mussels, some of which are found nowhere else. [3, 15] The establishment of both refuges resulted from long-term, collaborative efforts with local partners and conservation groups. [3] <4> [3] An agreement designating Oregon as the source for the initial 10 wolves was officially announced on October 6, 2023. [8, 9, 10] The long-term plan involves releasing 30 to 50 wolves over a three to five-year period. [5, 9] <5> The United States signed the High Seas Treaty, officially known as the Agreement on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ), on September 20, 2023. [1, 4, 8] The treaty, which is under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, establishes the first comprehensive international legal framework for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity in international waters. [1, 2] These areas, known as the high seas, constitute nearly two-thirds of the world's ocean and have historically lacked robust governance. [2, 13] The agreement focuses on several key areas, including processes for establishing marine protected areas, requirements for environmental impact assessments, and frameworks for the equitable sharing of benefits from marine genetic resources. [2] The U.S. signed the treaty on the first day it was opened for signature at the United Nations in New York. [1, 4] Signing indicates an intent to ratify and a commitment to refrain from acts that would undermine the treaty's purpose. [1] However, signing is distinct from ratification; the United States has not yet officially joined or ratified the treaty, a process which requires the advice and consent of a two-thirds majority of the U.S. Senate. [1, 7] The treaty will enter into force 120 days after it has been ratified by 60 countries. [1, 3] <6> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service released the summer 2023 issue of its quarterly magazine, 'Fish & Wildlife News,' on September 7, 2023. The publication summarizes the agency's activities and conservation efforts, with this particular issue featuring topics such as pollinator conservation and the work conducted by the Office of Communications and the Science Applications program. <7> Conservation groups and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) announced a historic settlement on August 9, 2023, aimed at bolstering the recovery of the world's only wild red wolf population in eastern North Carolina. [1, 10] This agreement resolves a 2020 lawsuit filed by the Southern Environmental Law Center on behalf of the Red Wolf Coalition, Defenders of Wildlife, and the Animal Welfare Institute, which alleged the USFWS violated the Endangered Species Act by neglecting its conservation duties. [3, 5, 6, 8] Under the settlement, the USFWS is required to develop and implement annual plans for the next eight years to release captive red wolves into the wild. [8, 10] These plans will be formulated in consultation with scientists and will include metrics to gauge success. [3, 8, 10] The agreement also mandates that the agency will continue efforts to manage the local coyote population to prevent cross-breeding. [3, 7] At the time the lawsuit was filed, the wild red wolf population had plummeted to as few as seven individuals. [3, 8] <8> The U.S. Department of Education's interpretation of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (BSCA) led to the blocking of federal funds under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA) for schools with hunting and archery programs. The interpretation stemmed from a provision in the BSCA, passed in June 2022, that prohibited ESEA funds from being used to provide training in the use of a dangerous weapon. This decision, which the Department of Education said went into effect on June 25, 2022, sparked significant backlash when it became widely known in July 2023. Hunting and conservation groups, along with bipartisan members of Congress, argued that this was a misinterpretation of the law's intent, which was to prevent federal funds from being used to arm teachers. In response to the outcry, a bipartisan group of senators and representatives sent letters to the Department of Education urging them to reconsider. Subsequently, in September 2023, both the House and Senate overwhelmingly passed legislation to clarify that the funding prohibition does not apply to archery, hunting, or other shooting sports training, effectively restoring the funding. <9> In response to a significant increase in Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) detections, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) adopted an emergency rule on July 24, 2023, implementing stricter regulations for the state's deer breeding facilities. The rule was enacted due to the discovery of CWD in nine different breeding facilities across seven counties in 2023 alone. The primary change requires that all white-tailed deer (*Odocoileus virginianus*) in breeding facilities must undergo ante-mortem (live-animal) testing and receive a "Not Detected" result for CWD before they can be transferred to another breeding facility or a release site. Additionally, the emergency order clarifies that official identification tags must not be removed from deer when they are moved to a release site to aid in epidemiological investigations. The temporary rules went into effect for 120 days, with a possible 60-day extension. <10> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) published a proposed rule to list the dunes sagebrush lizard as an endangered species under the Endangered Species Act. The lizard is native to shinnery oak sand dune ecosystems in southeastern New Mexico and west Texas. The proposal, published in the Federal Register on July 3, 2023, initiated a public comment period originally scheduled to close on September 1, 2023. Subsequently, the FWS extended the comment period by 30 days, establishing a new deadline of October 2, 2023, to allow all interested parties additional time to provide input.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) announced a Request for Proposals for its Conservation Partners Program on December 21, 2023, with a proposal deadline of February 28, 2024. [1] The program is set to award up to $12.4 million in grants for projects that encourage regenerative agriculture practices to improve wildlife habitat, soil health, water conservation and quality, and carbon storage on private lands. [1] An informational webinar for potential applicants was conducted on January 11, 2024. [1] <2> On December 11, 2023, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) released the Fall 2023 issue of 'Fish & Wildlife News,' its quarterly magazine. [1] The publication is written by and for FWS employees across the nation. [1] It covers a range of topics from the preceding months, including wildlife conservation, the recovery of endangered species like the Mojave desert tortoise and Rio Grande cutthroat trout, and various agency programs and initiatives. [1, 3] <3> In commemoration of the 50th anniversary of the Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, the Endangered Species Coalition released a report titled 'Ten Stories of Hope: The Endangered Species Act at 50.' The report, published on December 6, 2023, highlights ten successful case studies of wildlife conservation efforts across the United States for various imperiled fish, birds, plants, and mammals. One of the featured species is the Chinook salmon, which was nominated by the Sierra Club due to its significant ecological role in the Pacific Northwest. <4> The U.S. Department of Transportation's Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) announced the first-ever grants awarded from the Wildlife Crossings Pilot Program, created under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. A total of $110 million was allocated to 19 projects across 17 states. These inaugural grants are intended to fund projects, such as wildlife overpasses and underpasses, aimed at reducing wildlife-vehicle collisions and enhancing habitat connectivity for both terrestrial and aquatic species, thereby improving public safety and environmental sustainability. <5> On November 30, 2023, the Columbus Zoo and Aquarium and its partner conservation center, The Wilds, announced a major expansion of their conservation efforts with the launch of five new global and local initiatives. [3] These multi-million dollar, long-term projects aim to protect various species and their habitats. The five initiatives include: the North American Center for Bison Conservation at The Wilds, which will focus on herd management and prairie restoration; the Ohio Center for Wildlife Conservation at the Columbus Zoo, dedicated to the conservation of local species like hellbenders and freshwater mussels; a new Gorilla Doctors Center in the Democratic Republic of Congo to provide veterinary care for gorillas; the Center for Species Survival for Asian Elephants in Assam, India, the first conservation hub for this species within its natural range; and enhanced conservation efforts for critically endangered black and white ruffed lemurs in Madagascar. [2, 3] <6> The 'Fostering Overseas Rule of Law and Environmentally Sound Trade Act of 2023' (FOREST Act) was introduced as a bipartisan bill in both the U.S. House of Representatives (H.R.6515) and the Senate (S.3371) on November 30, 2023. The legislation aims to combat commodity-driven illegal deforestation by prohibiting the importation of products grown on such land. Importers of high-risk commodities, initially including palm oil, soybeans, cocoa, cattle, and rubber, would be required to prove their supply chains are not linked to illegal deforestation. The bill was introduced in the Senate by Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI) and Sen. Mike Braun (R-IN), and in the House by Rep. Earl Blumenauer (D-OR) and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA). The FOREST Act seeks to establish a risk-based framework for supply chain transparency, provide financial and technical assistance to countries to help reduce illegal deforestation, and create a federal procurement preference for deforestation-free products. The legislation is similar to measures enacted by the European Union and the United Kingdom. <7> After more than two decades of legal and scientific debate, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) listed the North American wolverine as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. [5, 9] The final rule designates the distinct population segment of wolverines in the contiguous United States for protection, citing climate change and habitat loss as primary threats to the snow-dependent species. [1, 5, 6] This decision, announced on November 29, 2023, and published in the Federal Register on November 30, 2023, reverses a 2020 determination that listing was not warranted, a move that was later vacated by a federal court. [1, 6, 10] The listing, which became effective on January 2, 2024, is intended to help conserve the remaining population of approximately 300 wolverines in the contiguous U.S. through enhanced viability and stemming long-term impacts. [3, 5, 7] <8> During its 2023 Winter Meeting in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, the Western Governors' Association (WGA) approved four bipartisan policy resolutions. These resolutions address strengthening the state-federal relationship, improving cross-boundary management of national forests and rangelands, increasing voluntary and proactive species management, and combating the opioid crisis. The meeting, hosted by Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon, featured discussions on significant regional issues including land management, agriculture, and improving the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) processes for energy projects. <9> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service held multiple public comment periods for proposals to expand hunting and fishing on National Wildlife Refuges under the 2023-2024 station-specific regulations. An initial proposal was published on June 21, 2023, with its public comment period closing on August 7, 2023. A subsequent, related proposal was published on October 26, 2023, for which the public comment period closed on December 26, 2023. The proposals aimed to increase access for hunters and anglers on public lands. <10> A multi-year project to restore the natural flow of Cripple Creek near Fairbanks, Alaska, culminated in success, nearly 90 years after its channel was diverted in 1935 for hydraulic mining operations. [2, 3, 4] The restoration, a partnership led by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and the Interior Alaska Land Trust, aimed to improve rearing habitat for juvenile Chinook salmon and other native fish, which was poor in the artificial, channelized drain. [2, 4] The comprehensive effort, which began in 2017, involved replacing and retrofitting multiple road culverts to allow for fish passage and ultimately redirecting water back into the historic channel. [3, 4] Key partners included the Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities, the University of Alaska-Fairbanks, local students, and community landowners. [4, 6] After a setback in 2020 when an initial diversion structure washed out, a successful implementation in the late summer and autumn of 2022 allowed clean water to flow through the creek's original channel for the first time in over 80 years. [4, 6, 7] By the spring of 2023, the historic channel was fully reconnected to the Chena River, marking a significant milestone in restoring the area's aquatic habitat. [6]

The move was celebrated by conservation groups, such as Defenders of Wildlife, which had actively campaigned against the delisting proposal. The commission's decision came despite a recommendation from some wildlife biologists to reduce protections for the species. <2> The Tribal Buffalo Lifeways Collaboration, a historic Tribal-led initiative, was officially chartered in June 2024 and publicly announced on July 17, 2024. [1] The collaboration aims to stabilize, establish, and expand the restoration of bison to Tribal lands, focusing on the cultural, spiritual, ecological, and economic revitalization of Native communities. [1, 3] The groups have also committed to working with the U.S. Department of the Interior and the Department of Agriculture to advance their goals. [1] <3> On June 28, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a landmark decision in the consolidated cases of Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce, overturning the 40-year-old 'Chevron Doctrine.' [2, 3, 5] This legal precedent had required courts to defer to federal agencies' reasonable interpretations of ambiguous statutes. [2, 3] The ruling establishes that courts must now exercise their own independent judgment to decide the meaning of a law, even if the statute is ambiguous and relates to technical matters. [3, 6] The decision has significant implications for federal agencies involved in wildlife conservation, such as the Fish and Wildlife Service, as their regulatory interpretations of laws like the Endangered Species Act could face increased legal challenges. [9, 11] While no existing rules are automatically changed, the ruling opens the door for new lawsuits against numerous agency decisions across the federal government. [10] <4> On July 1, 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced $48.4 million in grants to 19 states and Guam for land acquisition and conservation planning projects. [3] Funded through the Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund, these projects are set to protect over 23,000 acres of habitat for 80 listed and at-risk species. [3] The federal grants are supplemented by over $27.75 million in matching funds from partner organizations. [3] This initiative is part of the Biden-Harris administration's America the Beautiful initiative, which aims to conserve 30 percent of the nation's lands and waters. [3] <5> On June 5, 2024, a federal grand jury indicted a New York man on three counts, including two for smuggling and one for violating the Lacey Act, for his role in an illicit trafficking scheme. [3] The indictment alleges the man illegally shipped protected eastern box turtles and three-toed box turtles from the United States to China to be sold on the black market for the global pet trade. [3] While the indictment specifies China as the destination, these types of turtles are highly prized in the pet markets of both China and Hong Kong, where they can sell for thousands of dollars. [3] The alleged illegal shipments occurred between November 2019 and November 2020. [3] <6> As of May 2024, a legislative trend to bolster protections for endangered species was observed across the United States. At least 14 states had introduced a total of 24 bills with this aim. Among these states, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Washington have successfully enacted their respective bills into new laws, marking a significant step in strengthening state-level endangered species acts. <7> In 2024, a significant legislative push to enhance the protection of endangered species occurred at the state level in the United States. As of May 2024, at least 14 states had introduced a total of 24 bills with this goal. [3] Among these states, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and Washington successfully enacted new laws. [3] In Maryland, the legislature passed H.B. 345/S.B. 916, a comprehensive bill that expands the definition of "fish" and "wildlife" to include a broader range of species, mandates the Department of Natural Resources to review and update its endangered species list at least every five years, and uniquely empowers citizens to petition for the listing of a species as threatened or endangered. [3] Pennsylvania enacted Senate Bill 709, which specifically increases the penalties for any actions that lead to the death of bald or golden eagles, both of which have federal protections. [3] Washington also passed legislation aimed at wildlife conservation, including measures to ensure connectivity for wildlife through safe passages to reduce habitat fragmentation and vehicle collisions. <8> On May 3, 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, in collaboration with the Upper Colorado River Endangered Fish Recovery Program and Palisade High School's Endangered Fish Hatchery, held its fourth annual release of endangered razorback suckers at Riverbend Park into the Colorado River. [1, 3] Students involved in the hatchery program raised approximately 350-370 of the fish from the spawning stage and helped release them. [1, 3] This event marked a milestone, surpassing 1,000 total fish released since the program's inception in 2020. [2, 3, 4] Every razorback sucker released from the school's hatchery is inserted with a Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT) tag, allowing biologists to monitor their movements throughout their lives. [7, 8] The event, attended by students, partners, and community members, featured remarks from conservationist Jeff Corwin. [1, 2]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On September 13, 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) filed a legal brief with the U.S. Court of Appeals appealing a February 2022 court decision that reinstated Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections for the gray wolf in the continental United States. In the filing, the agency argued that the gray wolf has successfully recovered, calling the species 'one of the ESA’s biggest success stories,' and therefore no longer requires federal protection. This action seeks to reinstate a 2020 rule, enacted during the Trump administration, that had removed the gray wolf from the endangered species list. Conservation groups have criticized the move, highlighting what they see as a contradiction in the FWS's strategy, as the agency had previously announced its intention to develop a new national recovery plan for the wolf. <2> A coalition of 52 sporting-conservation organizations, operating under the name American Wildlife Conservation Partners (AWCP), has released the seventh edition of their policy recommendations, titled 'Wildlife for the 21st Century, Volume VII'. This document serves as a comprehensive guide for the upcoming presidential administration and the next two Congresses, offering solutions for wildlife conservation, habitat preservation, and public access. The recommendations, which are the result of over a year of collaboration among the partner organizations, are categorized into nine sections and encourage cooperative efforts between federal and state agencies, as well as private landowners. Every four years since its establishment in 2000, the AWCP has published this set of collective priorities. <3> On September 10, 2024, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced that the Migratory Bird Conservation Commission had approved over $46.2 million in grants. This funding is designated to conserve or restore 91,425 acres of wetlands and associated upland habitats for migratory birds, including waterfowl and shorebirds, across 17 states. The federal grants, provided through the North American Wetlands Conservation Act (NAWCA), will be supplemented by over $99.1 million in matching funds from partners. <4> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service issued a final rule to make technical corrections to the Lists of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants. This rule, which was published and became effective on September 10, 2024, corrects errors in previous publications regarding seven wildlife species and six plant species. <5> On August 16, 2024, the second anniversary of the Inflation Reduction Act, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) announced a nearly $20 million investment for endangered species recovery. This funding is part of a larger $25 million allocation from the Act specifically reserved for historically underfunded species. The investment will support recovery actions for four main groups: Hawaiian and Pacific Island plants ($5 million), butterflies and moths ($5 million), freshwater mussels ($10 million), and southwest desert fish ($5 million). This initiative builds upon a previous $5.1 million investment for these groups announced in 2023. <6> A final rule from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which took effect on August 12, 2024, updated the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife. This revision specifically amended the entries for five species of threatened Caribbean coral and added three nonessential experimental populations of Chinook salmon. <7> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) announced a proposed rule on August 1, 2024, to expand hunting and fishing on approximately 211,000 acres across 12 national wildlife refuges. The proposal introduces 53 new opportunities for hunting and sport fishing. A significant aspect of the proposal is that these new opportunities will require the use of lead-free ammunition and tackle. Specifically, the rule would mandate lead-free ammunition for all hunting on the new Big Cove Unit of the Canaan Valley National Wildlife Refuge in West Virginia and for newly opened elk hunting at four refuges in North Dakota. The proposal does not authorize any new use of lead. This move has generated mixed reactions, with some sporting organizations expressing concern that the lead-free requirement limits true access for hunters, citing the higher cost and lower availability of non-lead alternatives. The formal proposal was published in the Federal Register on August 2, 2024, which initiated a 30-day public comment period ending on September 3, 2024. <8> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced a proposed rule to expand hunting and sport fishing opportunities. Specifically, the proposal seeks to open or expand these activities on approximately 17,450 acres across eight National Wildlife Refuges (NWRs). The states impacted by this specific proposal include Alaska, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, and Washington. This action is part of a larger Biden-Harris administration initiative to increase recreational access, which includes 53 new opportunities across approximately 211,000 acres nationwide. This action seeks to reinstate a 2020 rule, enacted during the Trump administration, that had removed the gray wolf from the endangered species list. The recommendations, which are the result of over a year of collaboration among the partner organizations, are categorized into nine sections and encourage cooperative efforts between federal and state agencies, as well as private landowners. Specifically, the rule would mandate lead-free ammunition for all hunting on the new Big Cove Unit of the Canaan Valley National Wildlife Refuge in West Virginia and for newly opened elk hunting at four refuges in North Dakota. This action begins the process for a proposed 20-year mineral withdrawal. The area includes about 163,483 acres of National Forest System lands and 1,327 acres of Bureau of Land Management lands. The withdrawal is intended to prevent potential mining contamination and safeguard the region's water and air quality, cultural resources, critical fish and wildlife habitat, and recreational values, which support downstream agricultural users and traditional communities. <2> President Joe Biden signed the Coastal Habitat Conservation Act of 2023 (H.R. 2950) into law on December 11, 2024. This bipartisan legislation formally authorizes the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's (FWS) Coastal Program, a voluntary, partnership-based initiative focused on protecting and restoring habitats in 24 priority coastal areas. The program collaborates with federal, state, local, and Tribal governments, as well as non-governmental organizations and private entities, to provide technical and financial support for projects that assess, protect, and enhance vital coastal landscapes. The act authorizes funding for the program, with various sources suggesting amounts ranging from approximately $17 million to between $20 million and $25 million annually through fiscal year 2028, to conserve and aid in the recovery of federal trust species. <3> On December 9, 2024, at the White House Tribal Nations Summit, the U.S. Department of the Interior announced that 69 new Tribal co-stewardship agreements were signed in 2024. This brings the total number of such agreements under the Biden-Harris administration to 400. This report was developed by the American Wildlife Conservation Partners (AWCP), a coalition of 52 hunting and wildlife conservation organizations. It presents a comprehensive set of recommendations designed to guide federal policies on wildlife conservation and outdoor access for the subsequent four years, serving as a blueprint for the next two Congresses and the administration. <2> In March and April 2025, multiple reports highlighted growing concerns among environmentalists and conservation experts regarding the status of endangered species in the United States, such as the red wolf and the black-footed ferret, due to actions by the Trump administration. [1] Noah Greenwald of the Center for Biological Diversity warned that this could lead to significant habitat destruction. [1] Additionally, setbacks to recovery efforts were noted, including job cuts and funding freezes that could undermine the success of conservation programs, even those utilizing advanced biotechnology like cloning. [2] <3> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has proposed listing the monarch butterfly as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). [1, 8] The initial announcement included a 90-day public comment period, which was scheduled to close on March 12, 2025. [2, 8] Subsequently, the FWS announced it was reopening the public comment period for an additional 60 days to provide all interested parties another opportunity to comment. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service released the results of its National Visitor Survey, announcing that 97% of visitors reported being satisfied with their overall experiences at national wildlife refuges across the United States. <2> On September 18, 2025, the Department of the Interior announced the approval of over $54 million from the Migratory Bird Conservation Fund. The funding provides the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service with the resources to conserve 21,737 acres of waterfowl habitat and increase public access across four national wildlife refuges. <3> The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced plans to apply lampricide treatments to sections of Michigan's Paw Paw River in Van Buren and Berrien counties. The treatments aim to control invasive sea lamprey populations by killing larvae burrowed in the stream bottom, thereby protecting the Great Lakes fishery and maintaining the integrity of the ecosystem. <4> On September 12, 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced the extension of the Voluntary Lead-Free Hunting Ammunition Incentive Program for the 2025-2026 hunting season. The initiative provides rebates, including prepaid debit cards for reimbursement of lead-free ammunition costs, to hunters voluntarily using non-lead ammunition across 13 participating national wildlife refuges. <5> On September 10, 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced a virtual informational meeting scheduled for September 23, 2025. The meeting will update the public on the Red Wolf Recovery Program, including revitalized recovery efforts, the status of the eastern North Carolina population, coyote management strategies, and future planning to protect the critically endangered American Red Wolf. <6> On September 8, 2025, the Boone and Crockett Club released the findings of its multi-year 'Poach and Pay' research study. The report revealed that an estimated 95% of wildlife poaching incidents in the U.S. remain undetected, resulting in an annual minimum conservation loss of $1.4 billion through lost fines and animal replacement costs. <7> On September 5, 2025, a coalition of conservation groups, local fishermen, and community members filed a motion in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to stop the construction of Venture Global's CP2 liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in Cameron Parish, Louisiana. The legal action was prompted by a dredged sediment spill on August 4, 2024, which impacted at least 260 acres of marsh. Local reports indicated that the spill buried crab traps and oyster beds, and resulted in the death of local wildlife. The motion contends that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) unlawfully approved the project without giving due consideration to its significant negative impacts on coastal communities, commercial fishing, and delicate ecosystems. <8> On September 4, 2025, a federal appeals court panel in Atlanta paused a preliminary injunction that had ordered the shutdown of a mass detention center in the Everglades, known as "Alligator Alcatraz". [2, 3, 4] The 2-1 decision stays a lower court's August 21 order, which had required the facility to cease accepting new detainees and be dismantled within 60 days. [2, 7] This legal battle stems from a lawsuit filed by conservation groups, including Friends of the Everglades, the Center for Biological Diversity, and the Miccosukee Tribe. [3, 9] The plaintiffs argue that the detention center's construction and operation violate the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and cause significant harm to the sensitive ecosystem of the Big Cypress National Preserve. [9] While the conservation groups expressed disappointment, they have vowed to continue their legal challenge to permanently close the facility. [9, 10] <9> The Bureau of Land Management's Rawlins field office, in collaboration with Trout Unlimited, the Wyoming Conservation Corps, and the Rocky Mountain Youth Corps, has successfully completed a significant habitat restoration project in Wyoming's Muddy Creek watershed, a key tributary of the Colorado River system. The project, which spanned June and July, focused on enhancing the stream habitat for local fish and wildlife. Youth conservation crews were instrumental in installing 98 new beaver dam analogs (BDAs), repairing 40 pre-existing structures, and constructing a large riparian exclosure to improve water quality and create more diverse habitats. <10> On August 29, 2025, NOAA Fisheries issued comparability findings under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, providing full comparability to 89 nations to ensure that imported seafood meets the strict marine mammal conservation standards required of American-caught seafood.
